# An Evaluation Framework for User Experience Using Eye Tracking, Mouse Tracking, Keyboard Input, and Artificial Intelligence: A Case Study

Kennedy Edson Silva de Souza $^{a}$ , Igor Leonardo de Aviz $^{b}$ , Harold Dias de Mello $^{c}$ , Karla Figueiredo $^{d}$ , Marley Maria Bernardes Rebuzzi Vellasco $^{e}$ , Fernando Augusto Ribeiro Costa $^{f}$ , and Marcos César da Rocha Seruffo $^{a}$

$^{a}$Anthropic Studies in the Amazon Graduate Program, Federal University of Pará, Castanhal, Brazil; $^{b}$Institute of Technology, Federal University of Pará, Belem, Brazil; $^{c}$Electrical Engineering Department, Rio de Janeiro State University, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; $^{d}$Department of Informatics and Computer Science, Rio de Janeiro State University, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; $^{e}$Electrical Engineering Department, Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; $^{f}$Center for High Amazon Studies, Federal University of Pará, Belém, Brazil

## ABSTRACT

User eXperience (UX) has been used to achieve improvements in digital information systems based on how people perceive them. In particular, this paper establishes a framework that employs methods for eye and mouse tracking, keyboard input, self-assessment questionnaire and artificial intelligence algorithms to evaluate user experience and categorize users in terms of performance profiles. The results obtained with this framework are artifacts that can be used to support customizations of the User Interface (UI) on the websites. Moreover, the established framework is generic and flexible and can be applied to any information system, such as the case study shown in the website of the Federal Revenue of Brazil (RFB). The main objectives of this paper are as follows: (i) to set out a powerful UX framework based on three tracking techniques – the AIT2-UX; (ii) to provide the T2-UXT to collect, collate, process and visualize data obtained from users' interactions (iii) to use and compare machine learning algorithms with the classification of user performance profiles; (iv) to use the artifacts generated by the framework to manually customize the UI with the website.

## 1. Introduction

User eXperience (UX) requires an in-depth understanding of users, what they need and what they value, as well as their abilities, and limitations (U. S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2006). Consequently, UX best practices lead to an improvement in the quality of user interactions and perceptions with regard to goods and services.

UX is a growing field that is still being defined and includes, among other disciplines, User Design Interface. A better User Design Interface leads to greater user satisfaction with the web application, and hence, greater retention and revenue. The quality of UX design can be measured and evaluated by using appropriate tools for tracking each web user's activities (Egan & Filip, 2017).

Thus, UX evaluation is being carried out by means of different techniques and methodologies, such as smart-wearables (Pal et al., 2019), mobile games (Yu et al., 2018), facial expressions (Munim et al., 2017), gaze and mouse tracking (Peng & Liao, 2016), questionnaires (Schrepp et al., 2014), and others. The UX evaluation methods are key factors in ensuring that the development of goods and services is progressing in the right direction to meet the users' requirements (Rajeshkumar et al., 2013).

It is important to highlight that usability and UX are not equivalent concepts. A possible distinction can be made between usability methods that aim to improve human performance and

UX methods that aim to improve user satisfaction by achieving pragmatic and hedonic goals (Bevan, 1995).

Logan (1994) cited the most different concept of usability; he divided the definition of usability into two types: behavioral and emotional usability. Behavioral usability is one that deals with effectiveness and efficiency of the user. While emotional usability refers to the degree to which a product is desirable or serves a need beyond the functional objective.

Norman et al. (1995) defined that UX includes all the aspects of the interaction between the end-user with the company, its services, and its products. Morville (2004) says that the UX concentrates on having a deep comprehension of users; for this, is necessary ensuring that users find value in what you are providing to them. It is necessary to understand why they must move beyond usability and the facets of UX needs to be considered: Useful, Usable, Desirable, Findable, Accessible, Credible and Valuable. Therefore, to create effective and efficient usability along with an enjoyable experience, designers need to consider those factors of UX.

In 1995, ISO (International Organization for Standardization) defined usability as the degree which a system, product or service can be used by specified users to reach specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use (ISO, 2018). Otherwise, UX only got defined in ISO 9241–210 in 2010, as person's perceptions and responses resulting from the use and/or anticipated use of a product, system or service.

In addition, since Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been growing, with a wide range of applications and in different areas, this raises the question: How can UX be evaluate together with AI (especially Machine Learning - ML) to customize and improve the user interface?

In this paper, we consider the UX heuristics $^{1}$ to evaluate a website with our framework. We have proposed a methodological framework that includes a developed software tool. This is an improved version of the AIMT- UXT (Souza et al., 2019) and is now called T2-UXT (Tracking Techniques – User eXperience Tool) $^{2}$. It is able to extract UX metrics from the mouse, eye and keyboard inputs, which allow us to get new data visualizations, while the first version only collected mouse movements. T2-UXT has been integrated into the framework established for UX assessment to provide data capture using various techniques, and user profile classification via AI.

Several suggestions can be made, such as designing a model that provides parameters for customizations in the user interface. This type of model requires the following: (1) data acquisition, (2) pattern identification, (3) interpretation and (4) a personalized display of the system. In this work, AI will be included to help assess the relevance of features collected from end-users with different skill levels in performing Graphical User Interface tasks.

The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the related works and Section 3 establishes a novel framework. Section 4 examines the case study, generated artifacts, results and areas for further discussion. Section 5 summarizes the conclusions and makes recommendations for future work.

## 2. Related works

This section reviews the key factors in the studies that have led to the establishment of the framework. It is possible to list some examples of frameworks, case studies and tracking techniques that have employed in others works. In addition, is clarified the UX heuristics that can be used in the tasks to evaluate the interactions of the users. Finally, there is a brief analysis of tools similar to T2-UXT, which shows the differential of our tool.

## 2.1. Previous frameworks and case studies

Zarour and Alharbi (2017) point that UX frameworks provide a theoretical background for a thorough understanding of what UX is. This study tabulated the findings related to UX aspects and dimensions, until 2017, along with the measurement methods identified in a simplified UX theoretical framework. Zarour and Alharbi (2017) synthesize all the collected data into a theoretical framework, which suggested dimensions and the UX disciplines. The value dimension is the focal point for the dimensions of technology experience (TX), brand experience (BX), and user needs experience (NX). The context relates all dimensions together and surrounds them.

Table 1 shows previous frameworks focused on certain UX dimensions and aspects based on selective survey. It is highlighted that Tan et al. (2013) have developed a UX framework that focuses on user needs and its related aspects: hedonic and pragmatic. Their framework is based on a selected survey and Goal

Question Metric (GQM) paradigm, which is based on the assumption that for an organization to perform a measurement, it must first specify the goals for itself and its projects, then it must trace those goals to the data that are intended to define those goals operationally, and finally provide a framework for interpreting the data to understand the goal, according to Basili (1992).

On the other side, Changyuan et al. (2013) have developed their framework to focus on user needs experience and technology experience and their visual attractiveness, pragmatic and emotional aspects. Their framework, similar of this proposal, is based on defining UX under web environment. Value Experience (VE) is related to the studies that have been focused on the gained value.

Besides evaluating the previous frameworks to build a solid foundation for our proposal, we highlight the case study conducted by Basri et al. (2019) which proposes an exploratory study using the “think aloud” method and a set of interaction experience questionnaire to evaluate the UX when using the e-participation service on the Malaysian e-government website. Due to the arrangement of not setting initial tasks for the participants, they figured out how to navigate freely through the website and reported genuine verbal comments. The findings of this study point out that the number of problems encountered during interaction shows that people still experience problems when using the e-participation service on e-government websites. The study can help the Malaysian government to develop a more efficient citizen-centric e-participation service that eventually offers a good UX.

Thus, the frameworks shown in this section, specifically the works proposed by Zarour and Alharbi (2017) and Basri et al. (2019), provided support for the structuring of this paper. However, the AIT2-UX proposal, whose case study is presented, differs in some aspects from the previous examples in that: a) it is based on tracking eye, mouse and keyboard input, increasing the number of variables that can be collected from user interaction, thus generating more artifacts $^{3}$ that can assist in the manual customization of websites; b) it proposes tasks considering UX heuristics and a set of variables to collect user interaction data; c) the case study validates the framework and suggests a website customization based on the generated artifacts.

## 2.2. Tracking techniques

Regarding Eye Tracking Techniques, Sari et al. (2018) proposed a study that takes the fixation time, the time before fixation, and the number of fixations of the view points as factors for calculating the likelihood that a product will be purchased. The authors applied eye tracking followed by a questionnaire to determine the relationship between consumer interest in products and the range of selected products.

In (Zhang et al., 2018), the authors present a tool that measures a user's fixation time on dynamic areas of interest (AoI) through videos using eye tracking. This involves using a camera with an iris scanner and a monitor that displays the video. At the end of the video, a percentage of the gaze fixation time can be obtained for each AoI, which can be marked manually or identified automatically.

Regarding Mouse and Eye Movement Tracking, Aviz et al. (2019) present a case study in which they compared mouse tracking data with user gaze interactions to determine if eye movements faithfully follow a mouse cursor from a web page.

Heat maps were created to determine if eye movements follow mouse tracking. The results show that when eye tracking follows mouse navigation (dynamic behavior), task execution time tends to be shorter and, depending on the user's browsing habits, this tracking between mouse and eyes may be more latent. Thus, users with dynamic browsing habits tend to follow the mouse with their gaze, while users with static habits keep the mouse still and use their gaze to scan the screen.

Mouse and keyboard monitoring can provide a more complete view of the user experience under high cognitive load such as decision making and for carrying out tasks. Katerina and Nicolaos (2018) conduct an exploratory study to investigate the potential correlation between mouse behavior patterns or keystroke dynamics and a set of End-User Development (EUD) behavioral attributes. A field test was conducted involving 30 users interacting with a modern web-based EUD tool for building simple web forms. The results show that mouse pattern metrics such as random and straight movements, mouse fluctuation, etc. can be combined with perceived ease of use or usefulness, self-efficacy, willingness to learn, or risk awareness. Various key dynamics such as speed and stop time can be combined with perceived ease of use or self-efficacy.

In (Jiang et al., 2020) there is a study on the performance of different types of keyboard layouts that are specifically designed for an interface with touch devices. The goal is to understand movement strategies in a mobile keyboard input. Movement strategies emerged in response to the need to share visual attention: attention is needed to guide finger movements and detect typing errors.

Considering the correlated works on tracking techniques, the differential of our proposal is to combine the tracking of the eye, mouse and keyboard input from the data collection performed by a single tool. The same tool is also capable of generating more visual and quantitative artifacts than the works proposed in the state of the art, allowing manual customization of the evaluated system.

## 2.3. UX heuristics

Heuristic is an approach to problem solving that employs a practical method sufficient for reaching a goal, according to Myers (2010). In UX, heuristics defines of design principles aiming to improve the user's satisfaction and experience, consequently raising the chances of product's success overall.

Renzi (2017) presented a comparison of heuristics with different focus and necessities, considering (Nielsen & Molich, 1990), (Apted et al., 2009), (Inostroza et al., 2012), (Vilar Neto & Campos, 2014), (Resmini & Rosati, 2011), in addition to the 9 heuristics proposed by the author. Bader et al. (2017) analyze the current state of heuristic evaluation for measuring the UX considering, (Nielsen & Molich, 1990), (Shneiderman, 1997), (Väänänen-Vainio-Mattila & Wäljas, 2009), (Kientz et al., 2010), (Inostroza et al., 2012) and (Arhippainen, 2013).

Figure 1 shows the timeline of UX heuristics propositions over the years, considering the references as cited in Renzi (2017) and Bader et al. (2017). Each element shows the considered hardware context, authors' names and year of publication. We consider UX heuristics proposed in (Renzi, 2017) that are showed in the section 4.2. The Renzi (2017) UX heuristics are:

(1) Place-making – refers to the users' self-location in the system and within the experience journey;

(2) Consistency – the system has to present visual, typographic, information, action, and interaction consistency;

(3) Resilience – flexibility of the interaction flow and touch points in order to adequate to different users, different journey strategies and different contexts of use;

(4) Reduction - even if the back-end of the system is complex in its structure, the options and content have to be presented to the users in an objective and user-friendly way, providing reduced interactive actions and minimal cognitive workload on their journey;

(5) Correlation - the system has to go beyond semantic correlation;

(6) Equivalency to cultural conventions – it is important to understand users' references to technology, processes, understanding of functionality and interactions to use as a basis for developing a new system;

(7) Visual intuitive content – users must recognize functionalities, hierarchy, pathways and information with minimal memory load, by making objects, actions and options easy to recognize and understand;

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1. Timeline of UX heuristics. – Sources: Adapted from .Renzi (2017) and Bader et al. (2017)

(8) Natural, intuitive and direct interactions – any touch point of interaction with the system should be as intuitive as possible, by direct gestural manipulation or objective simple vocal commands;

(9) Contextual ergonomics – physical environments, contexts of use within the experience journey, and human physical limitations must be considered when designing interaction touch points with the system.

Considering the UX heuristics proposed by Renzi (2017), p. 4 tasks were designed, as presented in section 4.2.

## 2.4. Tracking tools

Regarding to the T2-UXT, there are several commercial and academic tools available that allow similar resources to be used. Munim et al. (2017) presents a study with the objective of evaluating UX through the analysis of users' emotions when using different applications. In this, the web-based tool was developed to capture the user's facial expressions, detect their emotions and, based on them, generate a report to evaluate the UX of the studied application. From the results obtained, the authors concluded that the tool developed is effective and efficient in the UX evaluation.

On the other hand, MouseFlow $^{4}$ tracks clicks, mouse actions, scrolls, forms, etc. This tool displays an interactive panel that shows how users interact with websites, since it is able to filter user sessions to detect problems related to frustration, errors and achieving compatibility. HotJar $^{5}$ was created for marketing professionals, product managers and user experience designers. This tool helps to analyze traffic data on non-interactive systems by generating heat maps, creating filters, and providing instant feedback, session recordings, and miscellaneous reports. CrazyEgg $^{6}$ helps to understand customer interaction on websites by creating heat maps and providing records of website usage. Visual reports are produced to learn how users interact, where they are coming from (location), where they are browsing and where they are getting stuck so that changes in design can be made in a reliable way.

The aforementioned market solutions are promising and can be easily adapted to different platforms. However, T2-UXT differs from them in important aspects:

(1) It uses a range of tracking techniques to evaluate the user experience: mouse, eye, and keyboard;

(2) It is able to provide a set of variables that can be exported for analysis;

(3) Is open source and free, unlike market tools that generally charge for their analytical tools;

(4) It was developed for academic purposes;

(5) It can allow expansion, adaptation, and integration with other tools, which is useful for meeting the performance evaluation requirements of experts.

Thus, T2-UXT is a more generic and flexible tool than the alternative solutions in the market. Following this, in section 3, the established Framework will be set out and the stages of its operations examined in detail.

## 3. AIT2-UX framework

A framework for the planned model was established, as shown in Figure 2, and comprehensively outlined in a step-by-step sequence.

## 3.1. Step 1: Planning

The first stage is to understand how the users interact with the system. The UX evaluation is obtained from the execution of Tasks by the users, proposed from UX heuristics, which basically determine which characteristics a system must present. Together with the definition of the Tasks, it is necessary to think of variables that store information about the interactivity of the user with the system.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2. Stages of the planned AIT2-UX framework.

Section 4.1 shows the variables of this framework. The definition of these variables was based on related works; however, the set of 12 variables was devised by the authors of this paper. It should be noted that, as in related work, the variables are sometimes called metrics. Regarding the Tasks, section 4.2 presents the 4 Tasks proposed to perform the case study, in addition to their descriptions and UX heuristics proposed by Renzi (2017) that guided their definition.

## 3.2. Step 2: Subjective UX evaluation

At this stage of the framework a traditional self-assessment questionnaires were applied. The users had to answer the System Usability Scale (SUS) questionnaires (Brooke et al., 1996). This is a single, reliable tool for measuring and quantifying the perception of usability in terms of efficiency, effectiveness, user satisfaction (ISO/IEC, 2011).

The choice of SUS was based on previous studies such as: (i) (Borsci et al., 2015) that assess user satisfaction in the era of UX, analyzing the variation in outcomes of three standardized user satisfaction scales, including SUS; (ii) (Kocabalil et al., 2018) that review six main questionnaires, including SUS, for evaluating conversational systems in order to assess the potential suitability of these questionnaires to measure various UX dimensions. The results pointed out in the studies include the relevance of using SUS to measuring UX.

SUS consists of a ten-item Likert scale (Likert, 1932) with five response options for respondents, ranging from “Strongly Agree” to “Strongly Disagree.” After the responses are collected, a standard conversion procedure is followed to form an overall usability scale between 0 and 100. A higher score indicates a more useful system and one which the users can more easily interact with. SUS has become an industrial standard to evaluate a wide range of products and services, including websites and applications.

To obtain results through the SUS scale, the following method is used, described in (Brooke et al., 1996):

(1) For odd-index answers, 1 is subtracted from a given user's score.

(2) For even-index responses, the response value is subtracted from 5.

(3) Add up the values of the ten questions, and multiply by 2.5.

(4) The final score is located in the range from 0 to 100, where 0 corresponds to a poor use experience, and 100 to a good user experience.

The method is represented mathematically in the Equation 1, considering Q as a set containing the 10 answers to the questionnaire, and i as the index of the answers:

$$
R = 2. 5 * \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {1 0} \left( \begin{array}{c c} Q _ {i} - 1, & i (\text {mod} 2) = 1 \\ 5 - Q _ {i}, & \text {otherwise} \end{array} \right)\tag{1}
$$

Applied after the completion of each task, the questionnaires collected information about the users' perception after navigating in the pages and concluding the tasks. This point is important for the training of the database, considering the profiles of the exercisers and non-experienced users, as will be presented in the section 4.4.

It should be pointed out that usability is a part of the UX and a crucial feature of highly interactive systems. However, for the determination of UX, other characteristics are necessary to be evaluated. Therefore, the questionnaires collect data that goes beyond usability aspects.

## 3.3. Step 3: User interaction data (T2-UXT)

The third stage is to collect the user interaction data from the defined tasks. This involved building the T2- UXT to capture and record the user's interactions with mouse, eyes movements and keyboard inputs so that they could be analyzed subsequently. Three key modules compose the tool: the browser, storage and data visualization, as shown in Figure 3, which allow the data to be to collected, collated, processed and visualized.

Figure 3 shows the user interaction, and how it generates data that can be captured by the Browser and sends them to the Server and Storage module, which is responsible for transcribing, collating, and storing the collected data with a PHP code. After the data has been processed, it is possible to visualize information about its usage and and user behavior through maps. The modules are displayed in detail in Figure 4 and subsections 3.3.1, 3.3.2 and 3.3.3.

## 3.3.1. The browser module

Figure 4 illustrates the architecture of the Browser Module (orange), which consists of three components: (i) Front-end, an Alias for the Web page view and its JavaScript code; (ii) the Browser engine, that manages the web page view; and (iii) a Data Grouping System, an extensive background submodule for preparing and sending data.

The Browser Module is a web browser extension implemented in JavaScript that handles user interaction and navigation events while the user is carrying out a specific task. The Browser Module can also record eye gaze positions with the aid of WebGazer library Papoutsaki et al. (2016). The recordings occur at a minimum interval of 200 ms, which is defined empirically to allow bandwidth savings for data transmission and also to preserve the data input accuracy.

JSON is used for intercommunication between the stages and modules because it is a standard that provides high-level data structuring, while at the same time, allowing interoperability between different languages and easy coding and decoding, even when performed manually. The HTTPS protocol is used because of its security and ease of implementation.

## 3.3.2.Storage module

The data sent from the Browser Module are received by the Storage Server (in green), as shown in Figure 3. Through an application implemented in PHP, the data are decoded and transcribed to PHP objects. Next, they are separated by single-user IDs and encoded in XML. Finally, the resulting data are stored in separate directories by domain and user ID for subsequent use in the data visualization.

## 3.3.3. Data visualization module

The Data Visualization Module is displayed in Figure 4 (in green). The XML files stored in the PHP server are checked by the preprocessor module, in accordance with Famili et al. (1997). The purpose of this is to fix any temporal inconsistencies and update the navigation records and, thus, improve the reliability of the samples. The processing resulting from this module is the basis for making alterations in an interactive system. Previously, this module required a C code for an automated treatment and exportation of the obtained data.

Regarding the XML file, Figure 4 shows some of the possibilities individually or by group, depending on the data obtained from any of the tracking techniques or a combination. DirectX graphical API and HTML5 are used for this Canvas to create visual representations of the data. The maps created for the case study of this Manuscript are shown in 4.6.2. The word cloud appears in Subsection 4.7.

## 3.4. Step 4: AI for data classification

During this stage, data preprocessing was carried out before the application of the Machine Learning algorithms. Preprocessing removes noise and variations that could complicate data interpretation.

Next, Machine Learning (ML) methods are used for this data. ML (Mitchell, 1997) is a major subfield of Artificial Intelligence that is essentially concerned with learning from experiences. Thus, each machine learning problem can be precisely defined as determining how to improve performance when carrying out tasks during the training experience.

In this work, ML was used to classify volunteers into “experienced” and “non-experienced” user profiles determined by the SUS questionnaire outlined in Subsection 3.2. These models also employed user performance variables in the different tasks from Subsection 4.2.

Due to this paper dealing with a small amount of data, traditional classification algorithms are explored, including Decision Trees, Neural Networks, and Support Vector Machines. Then, we focus on using a ML approach well suited to small data sets and strategies to increasing accuracy.

This step is discussed in detail in Subsection 4.3.

## 3.5. Step 5: Graph data analysis

In this step, the interaction data is represented graphically. In view of the many maps and graphs that can be obtained with the aid of the data visualization module (T2-UXT) – the AIT2-UX Framework -, Step 5 aims at selecting the data visualizer that can help to understand user interactions. So, this step provides artifacts that can be used to customization the UI. The generated artifacts are shown in the subsection 4.6.

## 3.6. Step 6: A suggestion for UI customization

Steps from 1 to 5 produce graphical and textual, quantitative and qualitative artifacts that allow for analysis and diagnosis of the system under evaluation. This makes the proposed framework an improved tool for identifying the source of problems in web portals. Then, in step 6, manual customizations to the user interface are proposed in the website case study. The procedure followed in this step is shown in Subsection 4.7.

## 4. Case study

The Federal Revenue of Brazil (RFB) website $^{7}$ was used when preparing our case study. Dozens of tax services are offered by means of this website, including Personal Income Tax returns (IRPF) and Corporate Income Tax Annual returns (IRPJ), the main source of tax revenue for the Brazilian government. Since the Government services website is widely accessed, the authors believe the RFB website is an optimal system for evaluating UX with the proposed methodology.

Volunteers with different levels of skills and knowledge about the RFB website were selected from universities in the North, South and Southeast of Brazil. The volunteers ranged in age from 20–60 years old, which is an economically active age group that generally needs some RFB service. Thus, it was expected that they would have a good UX performance.

Pretests were conducted with 10 volunteers, called initial volunteers, in order to identify which workflow could be applied in the tests. The pretest met the proposed objective; however, due to the fact that the initial volunteers had different levels of knowledge about the website and many did not even know the services that the RFB offers, not all of them were able to finish the assigned tasks.

Thus, the pretest was only used to idealize the tests protocol and, therefore, its results were disregarded in the database used in the other steps of the framework.

So, thirty volunteers were selected by means of the random sampling method Banuenumah et al. (2017). This meant that the volunteers were completely chosen at random and thus each volunteer had an equal chance of being selected at any time during the sampling period. Since the tests were conducted in different regions of Brazil (North, South and Southeast), a protocol of tests (Table 2) was established to guide all researchers/volunteers under standard testing conditions and steps.

Table 2. Protocol of tests.

| Step | Detailing |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Determined that the tests were conducted on three computers with an Ubuntu 16 Operating System and Google Chrome browser. |
| 2 | T2-UGT Browser Module was installed, which is designed to gather interaction data. |
| 3 | Each test session took place without any interference from other volunteers or researchers involved in this study. |
| 4 | The goal was to ensure the volunteers were entirely guided by the interface when carrying out their tasks. |
| 5 | Each task came to an end when all the assignments were completed. |
| 6 | For each task a SUS questionnaire was answered. |

## 4.1. Variables

The developed Framework uses variables to quantify user interactions. According to the interaction device, the variables are: (i) Mouse: variables that collect data from events related to the mouse device; (ii) Eyes: variables that collect data from observation points detected by the WebGazer library; (iii) History: variables that collect data and behavior patterns related to the browsing history recorded during task execution; (iv) Keyboard input: variable that collects user data during task execution. Table 3 shows the variables used in the Framework.

All variables were raised in the data collection of the four tasks proposed in the case study, according to section 4.2, except the variable Search words, which was collected only in Task 4. This refers to textual data collection. For classification models, all variables are included, except the Search Word.

## 4.2. Tasks

In this case study, four tasks are defined to obtain user interaction data. Considering that heuristics are used to measure UX (Bader et al., 2017), each task contemplates a group of UX heuristics, according to Renzi (2017) proposal. From the 9 UX heuristics proposed by Renzi (2017), p. 7 were addressed in the case study. The tasks are services frequently accessed in the Brazilian Revenue Service (RFB) website, e.g., the Individual Taxpayer Registry (CPF) services, such as registration, regularization and modification. CPF is a document required for both Brazilians and foreigners in a wide range of operations and legal proceedings (Task 2 and Task 4).

The difficulty of finding specialized services led to another task being chosen: the location of the e-CAC webpage (Task 1). This is a secure web environment (within the RFB website itself), through which a personal or corporate taxpayer can access tax services online, for example, tax consulting, tax guidance, any pending issues in the Personal Income Tax return, among other problems.

| Eye | Total Eye Distance | Distance in pixels traveled by user gaze when undertaking the entire task. |
| History | Page Returns | Number of times the user entered a page, ran a maximum of two more pages ahead, and then returned to the initial page. |
| History | Completion Time | Time elapsed from complete rendering of the page to completion of the task by the user. |
| History | Page Repetitions | Number of times the user entered a page already visited before. |

## 4.3. Machine learning for classification

After recording user interaction data, the next step is to build models based on Artificial Intelligence to classify the volunteers in experienced or no-experienced, according the features (variables) collected in the framework. The idea is to have a model that helps to understand the user classification when compared with another framework artifacts. For training the model, it was used a database created with: variables, that hold all interactions of the user; and SUS scores, that evaluated the user as experienced or non-experienced.

Machine learning is a major subfield of Artificial Intelligence that essentially concerns learning from experiences (Mitchell, 1997). Thus, each machine learning problem can be precisely defined as the problem of improving performance when carrying out tasks during the training experience.

Most machine learning currently involves supervised learning. This approach takes into account a finite amount of labeled data (and often noise) and recommends a superior behavior for the learning algorithm that is expected. If the desired outputs are discrete or categorical, there is a classification problem. On the other hand, continuous or numerical outputs denote a regression problem. The vast majority of studies on how to evaluate a classification model rely on predictive accuracy as the only evaluation criterion, i.e., the number of correct predictions for the total number of input samples. Thus, accuracy is defined as the proportion of true instances retrieved, both positive and negative, among all retrieved instances, as shown in Equation 2:

$$
A c c u r a c y = \frac {t p + t n}{t p + t n + f p + f n}\tag{2}
$$

Where:

$$
\begin{array}{l} t p = \text {true positive} \\ t n = \text {true negative} \\ f p = \text {false positive} \\ f n = \text {false negative} \end{array}
$$

Accuracy is an intuitive metric that measures the overall performance of a classifier and works well for relatively balanced datasets. Nevertheless, if there is a need to focus on a specific output class, alternative metrics such as accuracy, recall, and F1-score can be used. From the previous counts, one can calculate precision and recall mismatch with Equation. 3:

$$
\text {Precision} = \frac {t p}{t p + f p} \quad \text {Recall} = \frac {t p}{t p + f n}\tag{3}
$$

The F1-score combines the accuracy and recall of a classifier into a single metric, taking its harmonic mean as expressed in Equation 4:

$$
F 1 - \text {score} = \frac {2 \times \text {Precision} \times \text {Recall}}{\text {Precision} + \text {Recall}}\tag{4}
$$

Hence, this metric takes both false positives and false negatives into account. However, if the cost of false positives and false negatives are very different, it is better to look at both precision and recall.

Another way to display the results of a classifier's performance measurement and especially to compare several classifiers is through Confusion Matrix (CM). This is a Table that shows all four experimental results, given by $tp$, $fp$, $fn$, and $tn$.

Some of the most widely used classification algorithms are decision trees, neural networks, and support vector machines.

## 4.3.1. Decision trees (DT)

Also known as generalized classification and regression trees, decision trees are a way of representing a set of rules that form a hierarchy of classes or values, and expressing a simple conditional logic. These rules can be expressed in natural language, which improves the interpretability of the model for the user. A decision tree is based on a sequence of questions about the characteristics of an object. After the first question has been answered, the others can be asked until the class to which the object belongs is completed. The user-defined parameters include the minimum number of values in a node that must exist before a split is attempted, and the maximum depth of the tree that will be created.

## 4.3.2. Artificial neural networks (ANN)

In classification tasks, the free parameters or the synaptic weights of a neural network (Haykin, 2007) are learned through continuous interaction with the environment. The network is trained with input values and their corresponding desired output values during supervised training. Unlike decision trees, a neural network-based classifier does not decide in multiple stages. Instead, neural nets can be used to create a non-linear mapping from data features to allow new features of reduced dimensionality and better performance to be achieved.

One of the most commonly used neural network architectures for tabular dataset classification is the multilayer perceptron (MLP). MLP networks with a single hidden layer rely on a universal function approximator system and can solve any classification problem. Nevertheless, they have two main drawbacks: the difficulty of choosing good hyperparameter values and the poor interpretability of the induced models.

## 4.3.3. Support vector machine (SVM)

SVM is based on statistical learning theory (Vapnik, 2000). It is mostly employed for classifying nonlinear problems by finding the maximum margin separating hyperplane by using a kernel function to transform the dataset. The closest values to the classification margin for defining the hyperplane, are known as support vectors and selected from the training dataset. SVM is one of the most flexible and effective machine learning tools available, and has a high degree of accuracy. It does not suffer from the classical multi-local minima and is comparatively less prone to overfitting. SVM parameters have a significant effect on the overall classification performance. The proper choice of kernel, cost, and gamma parameters makes a huge difference to the resulting performance of the classifier.

Finally, in all the classifiers, cross-validation is essential for a good generalization. The goal of this step is to find the best model for user profile classification by establishing different frameworks, setting different parameters, and then comparing their performance in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. In order to do this, was necessary use the subjective evaluation. So, the results of the SUS will be examined in Subsection 4.4.

## 4.4. Results of the SUS questionnaire

The SUS score was used to understand and bear out the accuracy of the user profiles determined by the classification techniques outlined in Subsection 4.5.

The questionnaires are structured to obtain a measure of the users' perception of the evaluated system, such as, to verify if the SUS score of a user that reported “non-experience” is in accordance with the variables collected. This classification is also used to tag each task performed by every volunteer, allowing compose a useful dataset for training the classification model.

Figure 5 presents the SUS results, containing all 120 tasks performed by the 30 users. Confronting the SUS score results with the self-report field on previous experience (experienced or non-experienced) it was possible to identify that all volunteers who self-reported non-experienced had an average SUS score (considering the 4 user tasks) below 5. It was also possible to identify that task 4 presented the lowest average SUS score. With the case study database collected and the label characteristic (experienced and non-experienced) it was possible to generate data classification results.

## 4.5. Results of the AI models

This section examines the results obtained from the tests. All the scripts used Python 3.7.6, and the scikit-learn 0.23.1 library. The test results were tabulated for 30 users, with each user carrying out four tasks, making a total of 120 records (the dataset). Of this total number, 70% (84 records) were used to train, and 30% (36 records) were used to test the classification models. Table 1 presents the 12 variables that were defined to be collected using the T2-UXT; however, only 11 variables were included in the dataset analysis, since the variable “Search Words” is only used to create a Word Cloud.

The first step in constructing a ML model is to define the features of the dataset that can be used for learning.

DT, SVM and MLP were applied to divide users into “non-experienced” and “experienced” profiles. We carefully explored and evaluated the performance of these machine learning models using various values for their parameters.

Machine learning models using DT classifiers were trained with maximum depth of the tree in a range from 3 to 12. Another hyperparameter was the minimum number of samples required to split an internal node, in the (2–16) range.

The MLP classifiers considered one hidden layer in the networks using 1 to 7 units; solver (sgd, Adam, lbfgs); activation functions (tanh, ReLu, logistic); learning rate (constant, adaptive); initial learning rate (0.01 to 0.1); L2 regularization (0.0001 to 0.05), exponential decay rate 1 (0.95); exponential decay rate 2 (0.999); momentum rate (0.8 to 0.95).

Different kernel functions were specified to create SVM classifiers: linear, polynomial, and rbf with cost (0.01 to 1000), gamma (0.001 to 100), and degree (1 to 4).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 5. SUS results.

■ Task 1 ■ Task 2 ■ Task 3 ■ Task 4

All the previous combinations were evaluated using grid search with 6-fold cross-validation. Table 5 shows the highest F1-score for each of the three classifiers. The MLP achieved the best performance among all the models trained. This occurred when the model used: 6 hidden units, ReLu activation function, Adam optimization algorithm, momentum rate of 0.9, constant learning rate, and initial learning rate equal to 0.05. The best SVM classifier used the rbf kernel function and gamma equal to 5. The best performance for the DT classifier was determined using a maximum depth of 3 and a minimum number of 2 samples.

Furthermore, the DT classifier has outperformed the complex SVM and MLP models on the test dataset in terms of all evaluation metrics, as shown in Table 6. Next, the Table 7 shows the Confusion Matrix for this two-class problem.

It is clear that the main objective of a classifier is to maximize the tn and tp instances,"experienced" predicted as "experienced" user and "non-experienced" predicted as "non-experienced" user, respectively. As can be observed from Table 7 all the models correctly predict the 18 "non-experienced users" as such. Thus, the precision is maximum. Moreover, the DT model has the lowest percentage of "non-experienced" users who were misclassified as belonging to the "experienced" users class (fp). Thus the recall for DT is higher than for SVM and MLP.

In view of this, the DT model was selected as the classifier of the planned framework. It should be noted that all the tests were conducted several times with varying parameters to achieve a better configuration setup.

One of the reasons for the good result obtained by the DT algorithm is the fact that it intrinsically implements a selection of variables method (Gini). Besides, it allows observing the rules, extracted from the tree model, increasing the understanding of the features that lead to good or poor user performance.

The values of the variables (including typed words), heat maps, SUS Score, and machine learning results are artifacts that allow us to point out customizations in the evaluated web interfaces. The customizations are not yet automatic, but it is expected, in future work, to develop a new version of the tool, capable of doing it in an automated way, considering the collected UX heuristics.

## 4.6.1. Quantitative values of the variables artifacts

The values collected from the framework's variables, transformed into a table, allow us to understand the users' behavior when interacting with the system, by performing the Tasks. More comprehensive analyses that consider, for example, time to complete tasks and amount of clicks, can be performed in a comparative way to identify which tasks were easier to complete.

It is worth noting that the variable “Search Words” allows tabulating everything that was typed by the user when browsing the website. In this way, it is possible to analyze the most recurrent terms and common mistakes in search fields for information on the website, and word clouds can be suggested to help the user’s search process.

## 4.6.2. Heat maps artifacts

The heat map is a visual artifact that allows the identification of individual or collective behavior patterns. For example, in the case study tests, two clusters were identified: Figure 6a shows the eye-tracking of more experienced users whose average gaze fixation time to reach the goal of Task 4 is shorter. Figure 6b represents the group of less experienced users, who scan the screen more in search of the goal of Task 4, therefore, investing more time in its execution.

## 4.6.3. SUS artifact

By looking at the records of the SUS questionnaire (Figure 5), several analyses can be made. For example, it is possible to compare the results of the experienced and non-experienced SUS groups with the generated heat maps. In the proposed case study, Figure 7a presents the heat map of the mouse movement of an experienced user and Figure 7b presents that of a non-experienced user when executing Task 4. By consulting the SUS Score, it is possible to identify that these users scored 90% and 60%, respectively. In general, the SUS questionnaire artifact allows to ratify information from users or user groups viewed in other artifacts.

It is possible to check the values of the 12 variables collected and compare them with the SUS score obtained, individually or as a group. For example, more experienced users tend to take less time to accomplish the task objectives; then, it is possible to identify how much longer a non-experienced user takes to locate an object in relation to an experienced user. Also, with SUS, it is possible to identify which elements of the system users had the most difficulty in their experience, from the analysis of the questionnaire answers.

## 4.6.4. Machine learning artifact

From the training - with the generated model that has $94\%$ accuracy (using Decision Tree) - of a collected base of interactions with the website, it is possible to complement the table of variable values (Subsection 4.6.1). The classification of users helps to better understand the behaviors of users, or groups of users, when performing Tasks on the website. The model created for classification helps validate the other artifacts of the framework.

## 4.7. Suggestions for UI customization

System customization can be implemented for a variety of reasons. The RFB website is an interesting case study, as it concentrates many services on one portal, which sometimes makes it extremely difficult to find a particular service. Moreover, most people in Brazil use this site.

By way of validating the model designed for this paper, the RFB website could adopt custom screens for a specific campaign, such as the current year of IRPF. In addition to pointing out the value of the application, the Secretary of the RFB could devise a trigger for accessing the IRPF software manual, if it notes that the user is having difficulties in finding/ downloading the software on the page. The tests and artifacts generated (heat map and SUS Score) helped to reach this conclusion.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 8. Suggestion for UI customization – home screen (a)/(b) and search page (c)/(d) – from RFB website.

Another suggestion for customization is that if the artifacts indicate that the user is only accessing personal information, the system could hide corporate information, and vice versa. The Figure 8 shows a RFB website customization suggestion. The Figure 8a is the current webpage screen and the Figure 8c is the search page screen. Regarding the artifacts – heat maps and the classification model -, the Figure 8b display a new suggestion screen that contains all the objectives that can be accessed on the website, in a cleaner template. The Figure 8d shows a word cloud, which could be updated dynamically; this is based on the most recent accesses, and helps users find something faster.

## 5. Conclusion

In general, it was established that the AIT2-UX Framework can assist in making an evaluation of UX, by including multiple tracking techniques. The AI module can be used to identify groups (experient and non-experient) of users and the results can be used to manually customize the UI of a website. We have used this methodological framework to evaluate the experience of 30 users in performing four tasks on the Brazilian Revenue Service (RFB) website. The tasks were compatible with the UX heuristics proposed by Renzi (2017).

The three tracking techniques employed can get a great number of variables for identifying profiles. The mouse tracking is the most traditional technique and can easily be incorporated into other tracking systems. The tracking keyboard input can be used for recommending content and/or auto-completion. In addition, the history of typed terms can be used to create quick access buttons. The eye tracking is the most invasive technique – we assume it is a work limitation – since the user must have a connected camera (this could be interpreted as invasion of privacy). However, learning models can be only created with techniques available/accepted by the user. In addition, as the proposed model can be used in mobile devices, it does not seem to be a problem for the user to allow access to a camera device.

Since the AIT2-UX Framework is generic and flexible, it can be incorporated in the most diverse interactive systems and for the most diverse purposes. It would be possible, for instance, to locate the area of the screen in which a user has spent most time browsing an e-commerce website, such as the freight rate calculator, comparisons of products, or delivery time. With this type of information, our tool could assist business managers in making decisions, including where to make offers, issue coupons, or give discounts to customers. Thus, the AIT2-UX Framework can be useful to handle similar situations as those found in Navalpakkam and Churchill (2012) and Badea (2014).

Finally, it should be noted that the T2-UXT is a free and open source tool, that has been developed by a research team. Moreover its integration is simple, since it allows a wide range of online systems to be evaluated without any of the restrictions that can be found in similar solutions in the market.

In future work, we intend to investigate additional factors that may influence UX and build additional models based on Artificial Intelligence algorithms, including self-organizing maps, to improve clustering. Other machine learning models will be employed to compare their results. Moreover, we plan to design a new version of the tool, with features that allow the data of users belonging to a weak UX group to be processed. This will enable the system interface to be adapted automatically and ensure that this group of users notices that an improvement has been made in the UX.

## About the Authors

Kennedy Edson Silva de Souza received the Bachelor's degree in Information Systems from Federal University of Para, Brazil, in 2019, where he is currently pursuing a Master's degree in Anthropic Studies in the Amazon. His research interests include HCI, usability, user experience, and social technologies.

Igor Leonardo de Aviz received the Bachelor's degree in Telecommunications Engineering University of Para, Brazil, in 2020. From 2018 to 2019, was a scientific initiation fellow, being a member of the Software factory Lab where developed research in the area of usability, user experience, web development and app design.

Harold Dias de Mello is Doctor in Electrical Engineering from PUC-Rio. Professor at the Department of Electrical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Rio de Janeiro State University. His research interests are related to Computational Intelligence methods applied to decision support systems, pattern classification, time-series forecasting, control and optimization.

Karla Figueiredo Doctor in Computer Science from PUC-Rio. Head of the Computational Intelligence and Robotics Laboratory (LIRA). The research interests are related to Neural Networks, Fuzzy Logic, Hybrid Intelligent Systems, Robotics and Intelligent Agents, applied to decision support systems, pattern classification, time-series forecasting, NLP, control, optimization and Data Mining.

Marley Maria Bernardes Rebuzzi Vellasco is Head of the Computational Intelligence and Robotics Laboratory at PUC-Rio. The research interests are Neural Networks, Fuzzy Logic, Hybrid Intelligent Systems (Neuro-Fuzzy, Neuro-Evolutionary and Fuzzy-Evolutionary models), Robotics and Intelligent Agents, applied to decision support systems, pattern classification, time-series forecasting, control, optimization and Data Mining.

Fernando Augusto Ribeiro Costa master's student of the Graduate Program in Sustainable Development of the Wet Tropic and Specialist by Center for High Amazon Studies (PDTU/NAEA/UFPA). Tourismologist (UFPA) and Professor of Geography (IFPA). Currently research on violence from the perspective of the Necropolitics, in the Metropolitan Region of Belém.

Marcos César da Rocha Seruffo is Doctor in Electrical Engineering (emphasis in Applied Computing) from Federal University of Para. Actually, is Professor from Postgraduate Program in Anthropic Studies in the Amazon and Postgraduate Program in Electrical Engineering. The research interests are user experience, social technologies, interactive systems and artificial intelligence.
